rewrites.blindSummary:
This state/province, anchored by its capital, is the institutional counterweight to the country's resolution belt. On 6 February 2024 the capital's regional administrative court repealed the last remaining "against LGBT ideology" document in the country. The capital is the origin point of the progressive response: in February 2019 the capital's mayor signed a 12-point LGBT+ declaration (security, education, culture, sport, employment; drawn up with LGBT non-governmental organisations, including an intervention hostel and school support projects), which provoked the first anti-LGBT municipal resolution (in one municipality, March 2019) as an explicit counter-reaction. The administrative-court campaign, led from the capital by the national human-rights commissioner and carried through the regional administrative courts and the top administrative court, dismantled the resolution network nationally.

The unit's dark stain is historical: in May 2005 the city under its then mayor banned that year's equal-rights parade, and the international human-rights court (2007) ruled the ban violated Articles 11, 13 and 14 of the human-rights convention. This is 20 years past and has not been repeated; the current institutional trajectory is clearly positive.

Score of 0.56 sits 0.04 above the national 0.52. The only unit scoring above national in this dossier; well above the next-highest region (0.48) and the resolution belt (0.42–0.45), where the resolution legacy dominates and no equivalent court-repeal or declaration infrastructure exists.
rewrites.blindTangential: The 2019–2025 resolution fight and the regional bloc's funding conditionality concerned LGBT+ rights broadly (family-charters and sex-curriculum language rather than gender-expression enforcement) — their force for trans visitors is the institutional signal they carried.
rewrites.blindLocalsOnly: The capital declaration's operational measures — the intervention hostel for rejected teenagers and the school support projects — serve residents; a visitor uses none of them but reads the institutional climate they created.
blindSourceSummaries: An encyclopedia overview of the phenomenon records the full arc: by January 2020 a third of the country had passed anti-LGBT resolutions; on 6 February 2024 the capital's regional administrative court repealed the last document 'against LGBT ideology' in the country; by 24 April 2025 every anti-LGBTQ resolution and family-charter endorsement was withdrawn or court-invalidated.

A city-policy programme's March 2019 account of the capital's LGBT+ declaration: the mayor signed the capital's pledge of equality, non-discrimination and hate-crime response, and the piece documents the declaration's politics and reception in the capital — the 2019 commitment still shows no record of repeal.

rewrites.blindSummary:
This state/province is where the country's religious criminal-law wave began: its governor introduced the establishing statute on 27 October 1999, in force 27 January 2000, and by 2002 eleven more states followed — a parallel system of religious courts with criminal jurisdiction over adherents, which a 2025 government country-of-origin note confirms is still operative and capital-punishment-capable for same-sex acts. A 2019 rights-monitoring study of 173 religious-court cases from 2017 uses this state/province as one of three sample states, confirming the courts function in practice, not just on paper.

No capital sentence is on record as imposed here, and no trans-specific incident appears in the dossier; the finding is pioneering the bloc's enforcement architecture and hosting functioning religious courts.
rewrites.blindTangential: Same-sex conduct criminalisation is the adjacent layer here: the national same-sex-prohibition statute (up to 14 years, applies to tourists) plus the religious penal layer for adherents of the locally dominant religion shape police and morality-police posture toward any gender-nonconforming presence, even though the written offences target conduct rather than gender identity.
blindSourceSummaries: An international rights organisation's report (2004) on the extension of religious criminal law: this state/province's governor was first, introducing the establishing statute on 27 October 1999 (in force 27 January 2000); by 2002 twelve states had adopted some form of religious criminal law into their legislation — to date the only ones where religious courts have jurisdiction to try criminal cases.

A primary state/province-authored account of the religious-law adoption, written by the then top government lawyer and justice commissioner and presented at a religious-organisation-sponsored seminar on 6 July 2000: it details the enabling legislation — a religious courts (administration of justice) law of 1999 under the 1999 national constitution — which established religious courts with criminal jurisdiction and enabled the codification of a religious penal code, and records the chief religious judge taking over court administration from 29 June 2000 alongside policy moves against prostitution and gambling. It documents from inside the state/province government the adoption process that began the country's religious criminal-law wave.

An academic reconstruction of how the state/province's religious penal code was made: the governor appointed a committee in June 1999 mandated to study implementing the religious law including the full scope of its criminal law, and by the end of 2000 eleven other states had adopted the application of the religious law; the chapter analyses the codification of offences and punishments and the penal-code architecture the religious courts of the twelve states apply, grounding this record's claim that this state/province pioneered the bloc's religious-criminal framework.

rewrites.blindSummary:
This state/province is one of twelve in the country applying religious criminal law in parallel with the national system since the 1999–2002 wave. A June 2025 government country-of-origin note lists this state/province among those where the religious penal code remains in force for adherents, criminalising same-sex acts between men (death penalty the maximum) and between women (penalties up to flogging and imprisonment), with a dedicated section on enforcement and the religious police — the legal architecture, not a case record, is the finding.

No trans-specific incident, morality-police case or court-level study covers this state/province in this dossier; the bloc's own reporting caveat is that enforcement data capture only a fraction of actual cases, so silence is not evidence of safety. The national criminal code's coverage of men's acts (up to 14 years) applies here as everywhere in the country.

rewrites.blindOutOfScope: Insurgency-related violence and military operations in one region of the country affect all travellers in this state/province; only trans-specific risk is assessed.
blindSourceSummaries: An international rights organisation's report (2004) lists this state/province among the twelve states that had adopted the religious law into criminal legislation by 2002, with religious courts holding criminal jurisdiction over adherents beyond the national law.

A foreign government's country-of-origin information note (June 2025): the religious law applies to adherents in the twelve states and criminalises same-sex sexual acts both between men and between women; the maximum penalty for men's same-sex acts is death in all twelve states and penalties for women's same-sex acts range from death to flogging and imprisonment; includes a dedicated section on enforcement of the religious-law provisions and the attitude of the morality police.

An academic sourcebook reproduces this state/province's own statute on prostitution, same-sex conduct, brothels and other sexual immoralities (2000), gazetted on 18 October 2001 and signed by the governor on 10 December 2000: section 3 makes engaging in prostitution, a same-sex act, a homosexual act or pimping an offence; section 7 provides that any person who engages in sexual intercourse with another person of the same gender shall upon conviction be punished with death; section 4 deems all brothels closed on commencement; and section 9 assigns jurisdiction to the religious and ordinary courts. This state/province's own enacted death penalty for same-gender intercourse independently supports this record's finding that the state/province's legal architecture, not just the national framework, criminalises same-sex conduct.

An academic sourcebook's list of enacted religious penal codes records this state/province's religious penal code law of 2001, signed into law on 3 March 2003, with no operation date or gazette identified; the editor notes the text was obtained only in May 2006, after the volume's annotation had been completed, which is why this state/province is not among the individually annotated codes. Confirms this state/province enacted its own religious penal code legislation in addition to its secular morality law, so the record's claimed parallel religious layer rests on a state/province-specific enactment rather than mere umbrella coverage.

rewrites.blindSummary:
This state/province applies religious criminal law as part of the twelve-jurisdiction bloc adopted by 2002. The religious layer criminalises conduct beyond the national same-sex-prohibition statute, including same-sex acts between women; the framework applies to adherents, and its practical reach over visitors is mediated by arrest practice — including morality-police enforcement in the bloc — rather than by any formal 'tourists excepted' rule. No trans-specific incident or documented morality-police activity appears in this dossier for this state/province. Reporting-decay caveats apply: absence of records reflects fear of outing and surveillance gaps, not absence of risk.

Score 0.024 below the national 0.08. Tied with the generic religious tier of peer jurisdictions: the enacted parallel criminal system is the deviation, without additional case-level or enforcement evidence to push further. Well above peer jurisdictions scoring 0.03 and 0.02, which have death-penalty text or carried-out capital sentences respectively.

blindSourceSummaries: An international rights organisation's report (2004) lists this state/province among the twelve states that had adopted the religious law into criminal legislation by 2002, with religious courts holding criminal jurisdiction over adherents beyond the national law.

A foreign government's country-of-origin information note (June 2025): the religious law applies to adherents in the twelve states and criminalises same-sex sexual acts both between men and between women; the maximum penalty for men's same-sex acts is death in all twelve states and penalties for women's same-sex acts range from death to flogging and imprisonment; includes a dedicated section on enforcement of the religious-law provisions and the attitude of the morality police.

A news outlet (October 2023): a local enforcement agency raided a birthday gathering in this state/province that was preparing a same-sex wedding and arrested dozens of people; a local spokesperson said most of the men detained admitted to same-sex conduct and that attendees would be charged with the local moral-crime offence. The first incident-level evidence in this dossier that this state/province enforces its moral-crimes layer on the ground, with local charging of attendees.

A second news outlet (23 October 2023) independently confirms the same October 2023 mass arrest: a local enforcement commander confirmed the arrests after a tip-off about a same-sex birthday party and planned marriage in this state/province; a spokesperson said about a third of the detained men admitted involvement in same-sex activity while the remaining men and the women present were invited guests and onlookers, and officers voiced concern over the participants' ages. Archived from the live outlet URL on 4 December 2023.

An academic sourcebook records this state/province's religious penal code law of 2001, signed into law on 23 November 2001, and annotates its text: this state/province shares with three other states the same-sex offence punishing unmarried men with 100 lashes plus one year's imprisonment and married men with stoning to death; the offence for women carries up to 50 lashes plus imprisonment of up to six months; and this state/province defines gross indecency in its own formulation as 'any sexual offence against the normal or usual standards of behaviour.' The enacted statutory text behind this record's claim that this state/province's religious layer criminalises same-sex conduct by men and women beyond the national code.

rewrites.blindSummary:
This state/province carries both layers of criminalisation that define the country's bloc. Its 2017 secular penal code punishes 'unnatural offences' — covering acts between men and between women — with up to 21 years' imprisonment plus fine; and, per a June 2025 government country-of-origin note, the state/province's religious penal code additionally applies to adherents through religious courts with criminal jurisdiction, in force since the 1999–2002 wave, with the bloc's capital maximum for men's acts.

No trans-specific incident or documented morality-police enforcement appears for this state/province in this dossier, and no court-level study samples it. The finding is the stacked architecture: a long-term secular offence alongside a parallel religious jurisdiction, both current.
rewrites.blindTangential: Same-sex conduct criminalisation is the adjacent layer here: the national same-sex-prohibition statute (up to 14 years, applies to tourists) plus the religious penal layer for adherents of the locally dominant religion shape police and morality-police posture toward any gender-nonconforming presence, even though the written offences target conduct rather than gender identity.
blindSourceSummaries: An international rights organisation's report (2004) on the extension of religious criminal law: the first state/province in the bloc introduced the establishing statute on 27 October 1999 (in force 27 January 2000), and by 2002 twelve states had adopted some form of the religious law into their criminal legislation — to date the only ones where religious courts have jurisdiction to try criminal cases.

A foreign government's June 2025 country note carries a religious-penalties table covering the twelve states with this state/province's own row: religious penal code law (2002) with death by stoning as the maximum for men's same-sex acts and same-sex acts between women punishable 'at the discretion of the religious court judge'. The note adds that this state/province separately adopted its own secular penal code in 2017, whose section on 'unnatural offences' punishes same-sex acts and bestiality with up to 21 years' imprisonment and a fine, above the national 14-year ceiling. Dated government confirmation of the two-layer criminalisation this record claims: a harsher state/province-specific secular statute plus a parallel religious layer applying to adherents.

An academic sourcebook lists this state/province's religious penal code law of 2002, signed into law and coming into operation on 21 June 2002 (bound with the religious criminal procedure code), and records that this state/province is one of only three states whose enacted text states 'Whoever commits the offence of sodomy shall be punished with stoning to death' — with no unmarried/married graduation — while the offence for women is left to discretionary punishment. Enactment-level evidence that this state/province's religious layer is its own promulgated parallel criminal code carrying the bloc's capital ceiling for men's same-sex acts, confirming this record's stacked-architecture finding without relying on umbrella coverage.
